strengths: Addresses a well-known and practically important limitation of Equilibrium Propagation (EP): slow convergence and instability, which has hindered its adoption despite biological plausibility advantages.

The core technical idea—scaling down feedback strength (rather than forward weights) to control spectral radius and accelerate convergence—is simple, clearly motivated by RNN dynamics theory, and empirically effective, yielding order-of-magnitude speedups over prototypical EP (P-EP) while approaching BP-level accuracy.

Combining residual/skip connections with EP to counteract vanishing gradients in deep (up to 10-hidden-layer) RNNs is a useful extension, and the paper demonstrates it restores much of the lost accuracy (Table 2), including for asymmetric arbitrary-graph-topology networks.

Reasonably thorough empirical study: sweeps over feedforward/feedback scaling coefficients, network depth, symmetric vs. asymmetric connections, convolutional architecture, and comparison against P-EP, BP, and feedback alignment (FA) baselines.
Inclusion of dynamical systems diagnostics (maximum Lyapunov exponent / finite-time MLE) to characterize convergence behavior adds some rigor beyond just accuracy numbers.

Appendix provides a theoretical derivation connecting EP, local representation alignment (LRA), and BP under the weak-feedback/weak-supervision limit, which is a nice unifying contribution alongside the empirical work.
Reasonably well-grounded biological motivation connecting feedback regulation and residual/long-range connectivity to known cortical circuit properties.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to MNIST and FMNIST, which are small, simple datasets; despite claims in the abstract about applicability to 'large-scale networks that underpin AI,' no experiments on more realistic benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10/100, ImageNet-scale, or non-vision tasks) are provided, so scalability claims are not well substantiated.

The central mechanism (scaling spectral radius/feedback strength to control RNN convergence) is a fairly direct application of well-established ideas from reservoir computing and echo-state network literature (cited in Background), and closely related to concurrent work (adjoint propagation, Liu et al. 2025) that the authors acknowledge achieves 'similar' speed and accuracy—raising questions about the degree of novelty.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix different optimizers, batch sizes, and learning-rate schedules between P-EP and the proposed method (e.g., batch size 20 vs. 500, SGD vs. Adam), which confounds the reported training-time speedups; a more controlled ablation isolating the effect of feedback scaling alone (holding other training hyperparameters fixed) would strengthen the claims.

The manuscript's clarity suffers from numerous formatting/OCR-type issues and missing values in text (e.g., garbled equations, blank code repository link), suggesting the submission was not fully polished; some claims (e.g., 'weak feedback contributes to biological hallucinations') are speculative and not substantiated by any evidence or citation-backed argument.
The theoretical equivalence proof (EP ≈ LRA ≈ BP at infinitesimal inference limit) largely follows and extends prior work (Millidge et al. 2023) rather than introducing fundamentally new theory.

Limited analysis of failure modes or computational overhead trade-offs when using residual connections in very deep networks beyond 10 layers, and no wall-clock time comparisons are given for the deeper (5/10-layer) experiments in Table 2 as they are for Table 1.
No code repository was actually provided despite a 'Code availability' section, limiting reproducibility verification at review time.

strengths: Addresses a practically important and well-motivated problem: EP's notoriously slow convergence and instability, which limits its applicability to larger/deeper networks and hardware implementations.

The core idea of scaling feedback strength to reduce spectral radius and accelerate convergence is simple, intuitive, and empirically shown to give large speedups (orders of magnitude) over P-EP baselines while maintaining comparable accuracy.

Reasonably thorough empirical exploration of the feedback/feedforward scaling hyperparameter space (Figures 4-5, S1-S8, Table S1), including both symmetric and asymmetric weight settings and multiple depths.
Residual/arbitrary-graph-topology connections are shown to meaningfully mitigate vanishing gradients in deep RNNs trained with weak feedback, with ablations in Table 2 demonstrating the benefit.

Appendix includes a Lyapunov-exponent-based dynamical analysis (MLE/FTMLE) to characterize convergence behavior, and a theoretical derivation connecting EP, LRA, and BP under weak-feedback/weak-supervision limits, which adds some conceptual grounding.
Code availability is mentioned, supporting reproducibility in principle.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: scaling spectral radius/feedback strength to control RNN dynamics is a well-known technique (echo-state networks, reservoir computing, as the paper itself cites), and residual connections for vanishing gradients are directly borrowed from He et al. 2016; the combination with EP, while useful, is an incremental engineering contribution rather than a conceptual advance. The paper's own discussion section acknowledges very similar contemporaneous work (adjoint propagation, Liu et al. 2025) achieving similar speed/accuracy via low-SR random RNNs, undermining claims of substantial novelty.

Evaluation is restricted to MNIST and FashionMNIST, both simple, near-saturated benchmarks; no results on more complex datasets (CIFAR-10/100, etc.) that would be standard for evaluating EP methods (e.g., Laborieux et al. 2021 scaled EP to CIFAR-10). This substantially limits claims about 'practical' and 'large-scale' applicability of EP, which is central to the paper's title and framing.

The speed/time comparisons in Table 1 are confounded by multiple simultaneous changes (optimizer Adam vs SGD, batch size, architecture separation of output layer, activation function) rather than isolating the effect of feedback scaling alone; it is hard to attribute the reported '1-2 orders of magnitude' speedup cleanly to the proposed mechanism versus these confounds (e.g., Adam optimizer and larger batch size alone could yield large wall-clock gains).

The 'Ours-DLR' ablation (same hyperparameters as P-EP) shows much more modest gains than the headline comparison, suggesting that a good portion of the reported speed/accuracy improvement comes from optimizer/architecture changes rather than feedback regulation per se; this is somewhat buried and underemphasized relative to the headline claims.

Biological plausibility claims are somewhat overstated/hand-wavy: linking feedback regulation and residual arbitrary graph topologies to specific neuroscience phenomena (hallucinations, cortical connectivity) is speculative and not rigorously tested against any neural data; these connections read as narrative framing rather than substantiated contributions.

The theoretical derivation of equivalence between EP, LRA, and BP in the weak-feedback limit largely follows known results (Xie & Seung 2003; Millidge et al. 2023) and is relegated to the appendix without being leveraged to give concrete new predictions testable in the main experiments.

No comparison to more recent and competitive EP acceleration techniques beyond P-EP (e.g., Laborieux et al. 2021's drastically reduced bias methods, O'Connor et al. 2019's initialized EP), which are discussed in text but not benchmarked quantitatively, making it hard to judge whether this approach is actually state-of-the-art for EP speedups.

Statistical rigor is limited: many results are means over 5 runs without significance testing, and some comparisons (e.g., Table 2 differences of ~0.1-1%) are within what could be noise given the reported standard deviations.

The paper's writing contains artifacts (garbled symbols/equations e.g. 'β_i = ' missing values, broken citations like 'Journ et al. 2023', inconsistent notation) suggesting it was not carefully proofread, which raises concerns about overall polish and rigor for a top-tier venue.

Residual connections are only tested on very simple MLP-style RNNs with fixed layer width (64-512 nodes); it's unclear if these gains generalize to more realistic deep/convolutional architectures at scale, which is the ultimate motivation stated in the introduction.

The practical impact for neuromorphic/analog hardware, repeatedly emphasized in the abstract/intro/discussion, is purely speculative—no hardware implementation, no analysis of energy costs or circuit complexity is provided to substantiate these claims.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: EP's notoriously slow convergence and instability, which has limited its adoption despite its appeal as a biologically plausible, hardware-friendly learning algorithm.

The core idea—decoupling feedback scaling from feedforward scaling to reduce spectral radius and speed convergence—is simple, well-motivated by RNN dynamics theory, and empirically effective, yielding orders-of-magnitude training speedups while matching BP/FA accuracy on MNIST/FMNIST.

Residual and arbitrary-graph-topology connections convincingly mitigate the vanishing-gradient problem introduced by weak feedback in deep (10-layer) RNNs, with clear ablations (Table 2) showing substantial accuracy recovery.
Thorough empirical characterization using Lyapunov exponents (MLE/FTMLE) to quantitatively link convergence speed/stability to feedback scaling, going beyond simple accuracy curves.
Appendix provides a theoretical derivation connecting EP, LRA, and BP under the weak-feedback/weak-supervision limit, adding conceptual grounding to the empirical findings.
Reasonably extensive experimental matrix (symmetric/asymmetric, layered/convolutional, varying depths) with repeated trials and standard deviations reported.
Biological motivation (feedforward/feedback regulation, cortical topology) is well connected to the specific architectural choices rather than being superficial framing.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to MNIST and Fashion-MNIST, both small, simple datasets; no results on more challenging benchmarks (e.g., CIFAR-10/100) are shown despite the convolutional architecture being introduced, which weakens claims of scalability to 'large-scale networks that underpin AI'.

The comparison with P-EP in Table 1 relies on numbers taken directly from a prior paper (Ernoult et al. 2019) rather than being reproduced under matched hardware/software conditions, making the 'orders of magnitude' speedup claim less rigorous (different hardware, implementations, and frameworks could confound wall-clock comparisons).

Feedback scaling and depth-dependent optimal beta_i appear to require manual tuning per architecture depth (Figure 4, Figure 5, Table S1); the paper does not provide a principled or automated method for selecting beta_i, limiting practical applicability despite claims of 'practicality'.

The novelty relative to closely related recent work (e.g., Liu et al. 2025 'adjoint propagation', which the authors acknowledge achieves similar speed/accuracy via a related low-spectral-radius idea) is not clearly differentiated beyond stating the mechanism differs; a more detailed head-to-head comparison would strengthen the contribution claims.

The theoretical equivalence proof (EP ≈ LRA ≈ BP) is only valid in the idealized infinitesimal/weak-feedback limit, which is in tension with the empirical finding that deeper networks need moderate (not vanishingly small) beta_i for good performance—this gap between theory and the practical operating regime is not discussed.

Residual/AGT connections for deep networks still show a noticeable accuracy gap relative to BP in some settings (e.g., Ours-Residual/Ours-AGT trailing BP on FMNIST), and the explanation for the remaining gap is not deeply analyzed.

Minor clarity/formatting issues: inconsistent equation numbering and some unrendered symbols/values (e.g., missing numeric values in equations and text, such as 'β_i = ' or 'T_e = 00') suggest the manuscript was not fully proofread.

No wall-clock or iteration-count comparison against other recent EP acceleration techniques (e.g., Laborieux et al. 2024, O'Connor et al. 2019) beyond citation, so it's unclear how this method stacks up against the broader landscape of EP speedups quantitatively.

strengths: Identifies a concrete and practical bottleneck in Equilibrium Propagation (slow convergence/instability) and proposes a simple, low-overhead fix (feedback scaling) that yields large empirical speedups (orders of magnitude) while retaining accuracy comparable to BP on MNIST/CIFAR-10 and convolutional benchmarks.

Extensive supporting analysis connecting the feedback-scaling intervention to dynamical-systems quantities (spectral radius, finite-time Lyapunov exponent, convergence time), giving a plausible mechanistic explanation for why down-scaling feedback speeds convergence.

Residual/skip connections and arbitrary graph topologies are shown via ablations to meaningfully alleviate vanishing gradients in deep (10–20 layer) RNNs trained with EP, a previously unaddressed limitation.
Theoretical appendix relating EP under weak feedback/weak supervision to LRA and BP is a nice unifying analysis that supports the empirical findings.

Comprehensive set of ablations, robustness-to-noise experiments, and frozen-layer control experiments add credibility that learning in lower layers is genuinely functional, not just relying on a large final readout.
Reasonable reproducibility effort: code and notebooks provided, detailed hyperparameter tables in appendix.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: scaling feedback strength/spectral radius to control RNN dynamics is a well-known technique (echo-state networks, reservoir computing), and the core contribution is largely an empirical tuning of this existing idea within EP rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The approach essentially pushes EP into a regime where the RNN behaves almost like a feedforward network (as the authors themselves acknowledge in the discussion and appendix C), which raises the question of how much of the claimed 'EP' benefit is retained versus effectively reducing to BP/LRA with extra overhead; this weakens the central motivating claim that this advances genuinely recurrent, brain-like EP dynamics.

Evaluation is limited to MNIST and small/shallow CNNs on CIFAR-10; no results on larger-scale or more realistic architectures/datasets, and the paper explicitly notes an unresolved, non-trivial accuracy gap versus BP on CIFAR-10 with deep fully-connected networks, limiting evidence of practical scalability.

Hyperparameters (feedback scaling ranges, connection probability for AGT, residual topology) are tuned empirically per depth without a principled or automated method to select them, undermining claims of practicality for arbitrary architectures.

Comparisons to more recent, stronger EP variants (e.g., Laborieux & Zenke 2024's Jacobian homeostasis method, which also targets asymmetric/faster EP) are largely qualitative/discussion-level rather than direct empirical comparisons, making it hard to assess relative merit against the current state of the art.

The 10-hidden-layer asymmetric RNN with residual/AGT connections still underperforms both BP and FA substantially on CIFAR-10 (14% gap), and the explanation given is speculative, suggesting the method's benefits are fragile for asymmetric/random-feedback settings which are arguably more biologically realistic.

Some presentation issues: dense notation and algorithm blocks (e.g., Algorithm S3) are hard to parse, and important architectural choices (e.g., why particular residual connections in Figure 3a) lack justification beyond loose analogy to cortical connectivity.
The claimed extension to hardware/neuromorphic implementations is speculative and not empirically demonstrated; all experiments are run on GPUs with standard float32/64 arithmetic.

strengths: Addresses a well-known practical bottleneck of Equilibrium Propagation (slow convergence, instability) with a simple, well-motivated mechanism (feedback scaling) and provides extensive empirical characterization of RNN dynamics (spectral radius, FTMLE, convergence time) to support the intuition.
Demonstrates substantial wall-clock/iteration speedups over the prototypical EP baseline (P-EP) while achieving accuracy close to BP on MNIST and shallow CNN benchmarks.

Introduces residual/skip connections (including stochastic arbitrary-graph-topology links) to counteract vanishing gradients caused by weak feedback in deep RNNs, enabling training of much deeper EP networks (10-20 layers) than previously feasible.

Extensive appendix material: theoretical derivation connecting EP, LRA, and BP under the weak-feedback/weak-supervision limit; robustness-to-noise experiments; frozen-layer ablations to verify meaningful credit assignment in lower layers.
Biologically motivated framing grounded in a reasonably thorough literature review of cortical feedback/feedforward regulation and network topology.
weaknesses: The paper's own theoretical analysis (Appendix C) shows that under the weak-feedback regime that gives the claimed speed/stability benefits, EP degenerates into something equivalent to a feedforward network trained by BP/LRA. This raises a fundamental concern: the recurrent settling dynamics that motivate EP's hardware appeal are essentially suppressed, so the method may just be a roundabout, more expensive way of approximating BP rather than a genuine advance for physical/recurrent implementations.

Core contribution (down-scaling feedback strength to control spectral radius/convergence speed) is conceptually incremental, closely related to well-established ideas in reservoir computing/echo-state networks and prior EP work noting the need for weak feedback or differing learning rates across layers; the residual-connection extension is a fairly direct application of ResNet-style skip connections to RNNs.

Evaluation is limited to MNIST and CIFAR-10 with fairly small networks; for CIFAR-10, deeper/asymmetric models still show large accuracy gaps versus BP (e.g., 10-layer asymmetric with residual connections: ~30% vs. BP's ~48%), and the paper explicitly states deep CNNs remain unexplored, limiting the claimed practicality/significance.

Comparisons in Table 1 mix different optimizers/training schedules (SGD vs Adam) between the proposed method and P-EP, confounding the attribution of speedup specifically to feedback scaling versus other training changes (only partially controlled for via the 'Ours-DLR' variant).

No empirical comparison against other recent EP acceleration/stabilization methods mentioned in the discussion (e.g., Jacobian homeostasis, adjoint propagation), despite these being directly relevant competing approaches.

Several key phenomena are acknowledged as unexplained (e.g., why AGT connection probability peaks at P=0.2, why CIFAR-10 asymmetric-residual accuracy is ~14% below symmetric), indicating limited mechanistic understanding of the proposed architecture's behavior.

Hyperparameters (feedback scaling ranges) are tuned empirically per depth with no principled/automatic method proposed, and the method does not extend to sequential/temporal tasks, restricting generality.
Code availability link is blank in the submission, and while notebooks are claimed to be included, this reduces confidence in reproducibility as presented.

strengths: Addresses a well-known practical bottleneck of Equilibrium Propagation (EP) — slow convergence and instability — with a simple, well-motivated intervention (feedback scaling) that yields substantial (order-of-magnitude) speedups while maintaining accuracy close to BP.

Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple architectures (layered RNNs of varying depth, convolutional RNNs) and datasets (MNIST, CIFAR-10), with systematic ablations over feedback/feedforward scaling, spectral radius, Lyapunov exponents, and convergence time (Figures 2, 4–6, Tables 1–2).

Residual/arbitrary-graph-topology connections are shown to meaningfully mitigate vanishing gradients in deep RNNs trained with EP, enabling training of 10- and even 20-hidden-layer networks that were previously impractical for EP.

Solid theoretical grounding: the appendix derives the equivalence of EP, local representation alignment, and BP under the weak-feedback/weak-supervision (infinitesimal inference) limit, and this is empirically corroborated via cosine-similarity analyses of states and gradients.
Additional robustness studies (noise on weights/states, frozen-layer ablations) strengthen the claim that the learned credit signals are meaningful throughout the network, not just at the output.

Reasonable attempt at reproducibility (code and notebooks provided, detailed hyperparameter tables in appendix) and biologically-motivated framing connecting to neuroscience literature on feedback regulation and cortical topology.
weaknesses: The core technical contribution (scaling down feedback strength) is more of an empirical tuning/engineering finding than a fundamentally new algorithmic mechanism; residual connections are a direct, well-known adaptation from ResNet rather than a novel architectural idea.

The theoretical analysis (Appendix C) shows that in the effective weak-feedback regime the network dynamics essentially degenerate into a feedforward computation approximating BP — this somewhat undercuts the motivation for using a genuinely recurrent, equilibrium-seeking system, since the practical speedups seem to come from pushing the system toward feedforward-like behavior rather than exploiting genuine settling dynamics.

Performance gaps versus BP remain substantial in harder settings, e.g., CIFAR-10 with deeper or asymmetric architectures (up to ~14% accuracy gap for 10-hidden-layer asymmetric residual models in Table 2), and the paper explicitly acknowledges CNN scaling remains unresolved.

Hyperparameter selection (feedback scaling range, connection probability P, network depth-dependent tuning) is empirical/heuristic with no principled or automated method proposed, limiting practical applicability to new architectures/tasks.

Evaluation is limited to MNIST and CIFAR-10 with relatively small/shallow architectures; no experiments on larger-scale vision tasks, no sequential/temporal tasks (acknowledged as future work), and no actual physical/neuromorphic hardware validation despite motivating claims about hardware relevance.

Some comparisons (e.g., P-EP vs proposed) differ in optimizer (SGD vs Adam) and training regime, which complicates a fully controlled comparison of the core algorithmic improvement versus optimization choices, though partial ablations (Ours-DLR) are provided.
Presentation is dense in places (heavily populated tables/figures, long appendix with many sub-analyses), which could be streamlined for clarity of the main claims.
